headline: Ninety-Two Miles to Atlantis, One Bigeye, and a Chafed Leader I Should Have Checked Twice
subhead: The east wall gave up one good bigeye and a handful of yellowfin this week, but the run taught me more than the fish did.
body_markdown:
We left the dock at Montauk at 2300 Tuesday, ninety-two miles to the Atlantis east wall at a cruise of twenty-two knots, which puts you on the grounds a little after 0400 with enough dark left to set up a chunk line before first light. That's the math I run every time somebody asks if it's worth it — four and a half hours out, four and a half back, call it fourteen gallons an hour at cruise, and you'd better have a second reason to make that run besides hope. This week the second reason was a squid push building off Rhode Island that's been feeding bait onto the edge from Veatch clear through to Oceanographer, and a temperature break holding right where it's supposed to be for the second week of July — mid-to-upper 60s on the inshore side of the wall, pushing past 70 where the warmer water starts riding up over the canyon's edge near 39°49'N, 71°28'W.

We anchored up on the chunk in about 1,400 fathoms and started working butterfish and diced mackerel back on a slow flow, no weight, letting it sink and swing with the current the way you want it in that kind of depth. Bigeye showed on the sounder around 0500 — big, isolated marks holding deep, sixty to ninety fathoms down, not stacked but there. We hooked one on a bare 6/0 circle with a butterfish belly strip about two hours before color, fought it forty minutes on 80-pound fluoro, and lost a second fish twenty minutes later to a leader I hadn't re-tied since the last trip. That's on me. In this business you check your terminal tackle like you check your fuel burn — every single time, no exceptions, because the fish don't care how far you ran to get there.

Came daylight we pulled the chunk gear and ran a short troll spread — green machines and a squid daisy chain off the corners, a couple of naked ballyhoo down the middle — working the temperature seam along the wall. Picked up three yellowfin in the 35 to 50-pound class in about two hours of trolling, all right on that break where the cooler upwelling water off the canyon face meets the warmer surface push. That's the pattern right now across all four of these canyons — Atlantis, Veatch, Hydrographer, Oceanographer — the walls are doing the work, not the flat water in between. If you're running past the shelf edge and marking bait on the meter but nothing's showing on top, drop a jig — a 200-gram speed jig worked with a long sweep and a fast fall picked up two more yellowfin for us blind, no marks visible topside, just fish suspended over structure.

Block Island boats working Veatch this week are seeing the same thing — squid concentrations building up from Rhode Island and pushing out onto the canyon edge, and that's supercharging the bite the same way it does every mid-July when the inshore squid run finally reaches the shelf. I talked to one captain running out of Point Judith who chunked butterfish over a squid mark at Veatch in about 900 fathoms and had a solid morning of yellowfin, mixed in with one white marlin that came up on the long rigger and never committed to the bait. That's about where the marlin fishery sits right now — present, teased, not consistent. If you want a real shot at white marlin out there, I'd be running a dink ballyhoo behind a small Ilander on the shotgun and covering water rather than sitting still.

Hydrographer and Oceanographer are the longer commitments out of Rhode Island ports — figure 150 to 165 miles depending which slice of the canyon you're working, which for most boats means an overnight run both ways and very little margin for engine trouble or a weather mistake. Nobody's reported wahoo yet this week out that far, but the water's warm enough now that I'd expect the first real wahoo showing on the high-speed gear within the next week or two, once that warmer surface layer sets up fully over the canyon heads. Mahi have been scattered under whatever weed lines you can find pushed out along the edge — nothing consistent, a fish here and there in the five to fifteen pound range, worth a stop if you cross one but not worth burning fuel hunting.

Looking ahead, I'd plan the next trip around the weather window rather than the calendar. There's a front forecast to push through this weekend, and if it clears out Sunday night like it's supposed to, I'd run to Oceanographer Monday and work the same pattern — chunk overnight on the wall, troll the temperature break at first light, jig the marks that don't show color. If that front stalls or backs around, I'd shift closer and work Atlantis again out of Montauk, since it's the shorter commitment and the fish were there this week. Either way, check your leaders before you leave the dock, not after you've already lost the fish. I learned that one twice this week so you don't have to learn it once.
